The **Unitree G1** costs **$13,500** on Unitree's own store, and almost nobody pays that.
The figure excludes tax and shipping, it buys the edition you are not allowed to program, and for an American buyer it is the start of a bill that reaches about **$20,000** once a 40% import duty, freight and a customs broker are added - Unitree.

The most important difference between these robots is not size or price but whether you are allowed to **write code** for them.
The G1 Basic, the R1 and R1 Air and the H2 Basic are sealed: Unitree sells them as demonstration machines without secondary development, so you get the moves Unitree ships and nothing else.
Booster's K1 and T2, and every EDU edition, open the robot to your own software.
If you want to program a walking humanoid on the smallest budget, the G1 Basic is the wrong purchase at any price, and a Booster K1 or an R1 EDU is the right one.

We present SONIC-K1, to our knowledge the first open-weights whole-body motion tracker for the Booster K1 humanoid,
obtained by adapting the SONIC framework to this smaller robot.
...
SONIC [1] pushed this approach to 700 h of motion data and 128 GPUs.
The code is open, but it is built for the Unitree G1, and most labs cannot afford to train it at that scale.
Our lab works with the Booster K1 [2], a 22-DoF humanoid that is noticeably smaller than the G1, and we wanted a SONIC-style tracker for it on the hardware we have.
...
SONIC [1] trains a single tracker for the Unitree G1 on 700 h of motion data.
It uses per-modality encoders, a quantized motion token and a shared decoder.

results.snippet:
The Booster K1 is a 95 cm, 19.5 kg bipedal humanoid built for people who want to write the control code themselves.
...
The K1's only real competitor at this end of the market is the **Unitree G1**, and they are less alike than the price bracket suggests.
The G1 is bigger — 1.32 m, around 35 kg — with far more degrees of freedom, optional dexterous hands, and a much larger public software ecosystem.
It is also the most widely owned research humanoid in the world, which cuts both ways: the ecosystem is deeper, and on 29 August 2026 two vulnerabilities were disclosed in the G1 EDU allowing root-level remote code execution, one of them over Bluetooth.
...
No comparable audit of the K1 has been published, which is not the same as the K1 being safer.
The K1's case against it is size, price and durability.
At 95 cm and 19.5 kg it is a machine a student can carry, drop and reset alone.
It is cheaper at entry.
And it has the RoboCup evidence, which the G1 does not have in the same form.

The Booster K1 is a smaller, more affordable humanoid robot unveiled in October 2025.
It targets the education, STEM learning, and entry-level developer markets as a complement to the research-focused T1.

| Booster Robotics | T1 | 118 cm | 23-41 | 200 TOPS | ~$29,800 | 700+ |
| [Unitree](https://aiwiki.ai/wiki/unitree) | G1 | 127 cm | 23-43 | 100 TOPS | ~$16,000 | 5,500+ (all humanoids) |
| Booster Robotics | K1 | 95 cm | 22 | 48-200 TOPS | $4,999 | Included in 700+ total |
...
The T1's most direct competitor is the Unitree G1.
The T1 holds advantages in AI computing power (200 vs. 100 TOPS), lighter weight (30 vs. 35+ kg), higher knee torque (130 vs. 120 N*m), integrated audio hardware (six-microphone array), and faster stand-up time (under one second).
The G1 counters with significantly higher walking speed (up to 2 m/s vs. 0.5+ m/s) and a substantially lower starting price ($16,000 vs. $29,800).
Unitree's volume lead is significant; the company reported shipping 5,500 humanoid units in 2025 and has targeted 20,000 units for 2026.[1][6][19]
Booster's K1 competes against both Unitree's R1 and SoftBank Robotics' [NAO](https://aiwiki.ai/wiki/softbank_robotics_nao) in the education and entry-level segment.

content.text:
**Short version:** The **Booster K1** is the smaller, lower-cost choice for hands-on coding and teaching; the **Unitree G1** is a larger, more capable platform with a broader research ecosystem—but the base G1 is not programmable, so compare the K1 with a **G1 EDU** if you plan to develop your own software.[1][5][6]

| | Booster K1 | Unitree G1 |
|---|---|---|
| Size and weight | About 95 cm, 19.5 kg[5][7] | About 127–132 cm, 35 kg[5][7] |
| Degrees of freedom | 22[7] | 23 in base version; higher on some EDU configurations[6][9] |
| Software access | Secondary development supported across K1 tiers[7][9] | Base model is demo-focused; secondary development is for EDU configurations[1][6] |
| Price signal | K1 Geek advertised from about $5,999; higher tiers may be quote-only[6][8] | Base G1 listed at $13,500 by some sources; EDU costs more and is often quote-only[1][8] |
| Best fit | Education, competitions, and budget-conscious development | Research that benefits from a larger robot, optional hands, and a more established ecosystem[5][6] |

**Practical pick:** Choose the **K1** for an affordable, portable robot you can program. Choose the **G1 EDU** when the larger body, manipulation options, or Unitree ecosystem justify the higher cost; don’t assume the cheaper base G1 offers the same development access.[1][5][6] Pricing and included features vary by edition and seller, so confirm the exact configuration before comparing quotes.
